title: Problem 4.1
statement_text: Given a tournament $T$, what is the complexity of deciding if $T$ has a triangle-free FAS?
context_text: Aubian [6] raised this problem in the context of computing the clique number of tournaments (shown NP-complete in [6]). The $\mathcal{C}$-FAS Problem is considered natural because of its links with the dichromatic number and the clique number of tournaments, and because it defines natural classes of tournaments.
paper_contribution: Proves that the $\mathcal{C}$-FAS Problem is NP-complete when $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of all forests (a subclass of triangle-free graphs), strengthening related NP-completeness results but leaving Problem 4.1 open.
paper_title: Finding forest-orderings of tournaments is NP-complete

title: Conjecture 4.2
statement_text: There is a function $f$ such that for every integer $k$, there is a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a tournament $T$, correctly concludes that $\operatorname{\overrightarrow{\omega}}(T)\geq k$, or finds an order $\prec$ of $V(T)$ such that $\omega(T^{\prec})\leq f(k)$
context_text: A feedback arc set (FAS) of a tournament $T$ is a set $F$ of arcs such that $T\setminus F$ is acyclic. Given a total order $\prec$ of $V(T)$, the backedge graph $T^\prec$ is the undirected graph on $V(T)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc; the FASs of $T$ are exactly the edge sets of the graphs $T^\prec$. For a class $\mathcal{C}$ of undirected graphs, a $\mathcal{C}$-FAS is a FAS whose underlying undirected graph belongs to $\mathcal{C}$, and the $\mathcal{C}$-FAS Problem asks whether a given tournament has one. The dichromatic number of $T$ (minimum number of transitive subtournaments partitioning $V(T)$) equals $\min_\prec\chi(T^\prec)$, and by analogy the clique number of a tournament is defined as $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)=\min_\prec\omega(T^\prec)$, the minimum over all total orders of $V(T)$; so $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)\le k$ if and only if $T$ has a FAS inducing a graph of clique number at most $k$. Deciding whether $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)\le k$ was recently proved NP-complete for larger $k$, while deciding whether $T$ has a triangle-free FAS is open (the paper's introduction and conclusion give slightly inconsistent thresholds). Aboulker, Aubian, Charbit and Thomassé proved an approximation version for $k=3$: there are a constant $c$ and a polynomial-time algorithm that, given $T$, correctly concludes that $\overrightarrow{\omega}(T)\ge3$ or finds an order $\prec$ with $\omega(T^\prec)\le c$. The conjecture asks for such an approximation for every $k$.
paper_title: Finding forest-orderings of tournaments is NP-complete

title: Problem 4.4
statement_text: What is the complexity of the $\mathcal{C}$-FAS Problem when $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of all paths? when $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of graphs with maximum degree $1$?
context_text: A feedback arc set (FAS) of a tournament $T$ is a set $F$ of arcs such that $T\setminus F$ is acyclic. Given a total order $\prec$ of $V(T)$, the backedge graph $T^\prec$ is the undirected graph on $V(T)$ with an edge $uv$ whenever $u\prec v$ and $vu$ is an arc; the FASs of $T$ are exactly the edge sets of the graphs $T^\prec$. For a class $\mathcal{C}$ of undirected graphs, a $\mathcal{C}$-FAS is a FAS whose underlying undirected graph belongs to $\mathcal{C}$, and the $\mathcal{C}$-FAS Problem asks whether a given tournament has one. The authors prove that the $\mathcal{C}$-FAS Problem is NP-complete when $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of forests (by reduction from 3-SAT), and hence also for trees, since a tournament has a forest-ordering if and only if it has a tree-ordering. Deciding whether a tournament is $k$-dicolourable is the $\mathcal{C}$-FAS Problem for $k$-colourable graphs, NP-complete for every $k\ge2$, and Chen et al. showed it is NP-complete to decide whether a tournament has a bipartite backedge graph. It is natural to ask for which classes $\mathcal{C}$ the problem is in P; paths and matchings (graphs of maximum degree at most 1) are two natural candidates. Related motivation: Chudnovsky et al. conjectured that a tournament has the strong Erdős–Hajnal property if and only if it has a FAS inducing a forest.
paper_title: Finding forest-orderings of tournaments is NP-complete
